subject: Astronomy & Space
title: What Is an Exoplanet?
description: One-minute skill: What Is an Exoplanet?.

hook.text: An exoplanet is any planet that orbits a star other than the Sun. Over 5,600 have been confirmed so far.

buildup.text: For centuries, scientists suspected other stars had planets, but proof was impossible with old telescopes.

discovery.text: The first confirmed exoplanets were found in 1992—orbiting a pulsar, not a normal star. Nobody expected that.

twist.text: The first exoplanet around a Sun-like star came in 1995. 51 Pegasi b was a giant planet orbiting absurdly close to its star.

climax.text: Now we know planets are common. Statistically, every star in the Milky Way hosts at least one planet.

punchline.text: Five thousand worlds and counting. Planets are the rule, not the exception.

quiz.question: Where were the first confirmed exoplanets found?
options: Orbiting a pulsar, not a Sun-like star
Orbiting the nearest star to the Sun, Proxima Centauri
Floating freely in space with no star at all

details.summary: An exoplanet is any planet orbiting a star other than our Sun. The first confirmed exoplanet around a Sun-like star was 51 Pegasi b, discovered in 1995.
details.whyItMatters: Exoplanet discovery transformed astronomy by proving that planets are ubiquitous. Finding them addresses one of humanity's oldest questions: are there other worlds like Earth, and could they harbor life?
takeaways: Exoplanets orbit stars beyond our solar system
Over 5,600 confirmed since the first discovery in 1995

faq.question: How are most exoplanets discovered?
faq.answer: The transit method dominates — it detects the tiny dimming when a planet crosses in front of its star. NASA's Kepler and TESS missions used this technique to find thousands.

faq.question: Are exoplanets common in the galaxy?
faq.answer: Extremely common. Statistical analysis of Kepler data suggests there are more planets than stars in the Milky Way — likely over 100 billion planets. On average, every star has at least one planet, and roughly one in five Sun-like stars has an Earth-sized planet in the habitable zone.
